How do scope and lifetime differ?
column2:
Scope determines where a name can be used. Lifetime determines when an object exists. A local static object can outlive the block in which its name is visible.

void Count() {
    static int count = 0;
    ++count;
} // count keeps its value between calls
// The name count is not accessible here.

column1: What happens when an inner scope declares a name already used in an outer scope?
column2:
The inner declaration hides the outer name within its scope. It creates a distinct variable; it does not replace or modify the outer object. Avoid unnecessary shadowing.

int value = 10;
{
    int value = 20; // different object
    ++value;       // inner value becomes 21
}
// Outer value is still 10.

column1: What is the difference between a type, an object, a variable, and a literal?
column2:
A type specifies values and operations. An object is storage holding a value of a type. In this simple case, a variable names an object. A literal is source notation for a value; an integer literal is not itself a separate object.

int count = 5;
// int: type
// count: variable naming an int object
// 5: integer literal denoting the value five

column1: How does initialization differ from assignment?
column2:
Initialization establishes an object when it is created. Assignment changes an existing object. The symbol = can appear in both; its presence alone does not mean assignment.

int value = 7; // initialization
value = 9;     // assignment
int other{7};  // initialization

column1: How do uninitialized automatic and static int variables differ?
column2:
An ordinary local int without an initializer has an indeterminate value; reading that value is undefined behavior in C++20. Assigning a value first is valid. A static int without an explicit initializer is zero-initialized.

void Example() {
    int local;
    local = 5;       // OK: writing before reading
    static int shared; // initially 0; survives calls
}
// Prefer int local{} when zero is wanted.

column1: Does assigning to a reference change which object it refers to?
column2:
No. A reference must be bound during initialization and cannot be reseated. Assignment through it changes the referred-to object.

int a = 1;
int b = 2;
int& ref = a;
ref = b; // a becomes 2; ref still refers to a
// int& missing; // error: no initializer

column1: What is copied when one raw pointer is assigned to another?
column2:
The address value is copied, not the pointed-to object. The pointers are distinct variables that can point to the same object. Reassigning one pointer does not reassign the other.

int a = 1, b = 2;
int* p = &a;
int* q = &b;
p = q;  // both point to b
*p = 9; // b becomes 9
p = &a; // q still points to b

column1: How does pointer arithmetic relate to array layout?
column2:
Array elements are contiguous. Moving a T pointer by one moves to the next T element, a distance of sizeof(T) bytes. Pointer arithmetic must stay within the same array or its one-past position.

int values[]{10, 20, 30};
int* p = &values[0];
++p; // points to values[1]
// *p == 20
// p[i] means *(p + i).

column1: Which array positions may be accessed, and what is a one-past pointer for?
column2:
For an array of N elements, valid indices are 0 through N-1. A pointer one past the array may be formed and used as an iteration boundary, but not dereferenced. Built-in array indexing does not check bounds.

int values[3]{};
int* end = values + 3; // valid boundary
values[2] = 7;         // OK
// *end = 7;           // undefined behavior
// values[3] = 7;      // undefined behavior

column1: Does checking a pointer against nullptr prove that it is safe to dereference?
column2:
No. It proves only that the pointer is not null. A non-null pointer can still be dangling or one-past an array. Dereferencing requires a live, accessible object of an appropriate type.

int* p = nullptr;
if (p) {
    // This branch is skipped.
}
// Never dereference nullptr.
// A dangling pointer is not automatically set to nullptr.

column1: How does a C-style string terminator differ from nullptr?
column2:
A C-style string ends with a zero-valued character, '\0'. nullptr is a null pointer value, not a character. Character-by-character traversal needs an accessible terminator to know where to stop.

const char* text = "Hi"; // H, i, then '\0'
while (*text != '\0') {
    ++text;
}
// text points to the terminator; it is not nullptr.

column1: Does a const reference make the original object immutable?
column2:
It prevents modification through that reference. If the original object is non-const, another non-const name or reference can still modify it. Use const references to provide read-only access without copying.

int value = 1;
const int& view = value;
// view = 2; // error
value = 2;   // OK; view now observes 2

column1: How does consteval differ from constexpr for function calls?
column2:
A constexpr function supports both constant and runtime evaluation. An ordinary call to a consteval function must be a constant expression, even if its result is assigned to a non-constexpr variable.

consteval int Twice(int x) { return x * 2; }
int a = Twice(3); // OK: evaluated at compile time
int input = ReadInput();
// int b = Twice(input); // error: runtime argument

column1: Where does C++ require constant expressions rather than runtime values?
column2:
Examples include built-in array bounds, case labels, non-type template arguments, and constexpr variable initializers. Const alone does not guarantee that an expression qualifies.

constexpr int size = 4;
int values[size]; // OK
const int runtimeSize = ReadInput();
// int other[runtimeSize]; // not standard C++
// A local const int initialized with 4 would qualify.

column1: Can constant evaluation modify existing global state?
column2:
No. A required constant evaluation cannot modify an existing global object. It can modify local objects created within that evaluation. A constexpr function is not necessarily side-effect-free when called at runtime.

int counter = 0;
constexpr int Compute(int x) {
    if (x > 0) ++counter;
    return x * 2;
}
constexpr int a = Compute(0); // OK
// constexpr int b = Compute(1); // error
int c = Compute(1); // OK: runtime; increments counter

column1: Where is a variable declared in an if initializer available?
column2:
It is available in the condition and both branches of that if statement, but not after the statement. This limits scope and prevents accidental later use.

if (auto n = values.size(); n != 0) {
    Print(n);
} else {
    Print(n); // also in scope
}
// Print(n); // error: n is out of scope

column1: How do break and return differ inside a switch nested in a loop?
column2:
break exits the nearest enclosing loop or switch; inside a switch it exits that switch, not an outer loop. return exits the entire function. Without an exit, execution can fall through into the next case.

for (char command : commands) {
    switch (command) {
    case 's': Save(); break; // continues after switch
    case 'q': return;       // leaves the function
    default: break;
    }
    Refresh();
}

column1: How do machine addresses, registers, and language-level objects relate?
column2:
A pointer typically represents a virtual memory address. CPU registers hold current values and addresses; cache and RAM serve memory accesses. A C++ object does not imply a separate RAM slot: optimization can keep values in registers or eliminate unused objects.

int value = 5;
int result = value + 1;
// No fixed number of RAM loads/stores is guaranteed.
// Choose value/reference semantics for behavior first.
